Into the Helix

A dying star: its photograph, its shape in 3D and its heart. Then back to Earth.

Open the trip: Into the Helix

The Helix Nebula, as a telescope sees it

This photograph from Chile lines up with our sky. At its centre a star like the Sun is dying. Gaia, a spacecraft, measured its yearly shift: it is 655 light-years away.

Turn, and the photograph becomes a shape

As we turn, the photograph fades and a model takes over. Robert O'Dell and colleagues measured how the gas moves, and found a disc inside a ring tilted almost across it. This is their reconstruction.

Inside the ring, around the dying star

Inside the ring we face the dying star: a white dwarf of about a hundred thousand degrees. Its dark knots, each wider than our Solar System, are real; where each sits is made up.

How big it is

The bright ring is nearly two and a half light-years across; in our sky the nebula is almost as wide as the full Moon, but too faint for the eye. Its light left 655 years ago.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the HYG star database, OpenNGC and the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
